summary: An end-to-end, intermediate-level guide to running the Qwen3.6 35B A3B mixture-of-experts model locally with llama.cpp and managing it as a systemd service. The lesson opens with a quick architectural orientation: 35B total parameters but only 3B active per token, 256 experts with 8 routed plus 1 shared firing per forward pass, a native 262K-token context window, and an Unsloth GGUF release with quantisations spanning 10 GB to 70 GB. The first concrete step builds llama.cpp from source on Debian/Ubuntu, with the CUDA backend enabled (-DGGML_CUDA=ON) and libcurl support (-DLLAMA_CURL=ON) so that llama-server can resolve Hugging Face shortcuts like unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GGUF:UD-Q4_K_M directly. The second step walks through three ways to get the weights — the built-in -hf shortcut, huggingface-cli download for explicit paths, and direct LFS URLs — alongside a quantisation table mapping VRAM budgets to specific tags (UD-IQ2_M for 12 GB, UD-Q3_K_M for 16 GB, UD-Q4_K_M for 24 GB, Q8_0 and BF16 for larger setups). The third step explains the six load-bearing llama-server flags: --model, --host/--port, --ctx-size, --n-gpu-layers, --threads/--threads-batch, --batch-size/--ubatch-size, --parallel, --jinja, and --api-key, including the often-missed detail that context size is divided across parallel slots. The fourth step is the MoE-specific tuning section that pays the rent: the routed experts are the bulk of the weights but rarely used, so --cpu-moe pushes all of them to CPU, --n-cpu-moe N pushes the first N layers' experts, and --override-tensor "exps=CPU" gives regex-level control, letting a 22 GB Q4 model run on a 12 GB card or a full 64K context on a 24 GB card. The fifth step verifies the live endpoint by hand with curl against /v1/models and /v1/chat/completions, confirming the OpenAI-compatible shape. The sixth step wraps everything in a systemd service: a dedicated 'llama' system user, a locked-down /etc/llama-server.env containing the API key and tunable parameters, a unit file with After=network-online.target, Restart=on-failure, a generous TimeoutStartSec for the slow GGUF load, and a sandboxing block (NoNewPrivileges, ProtectSystem=strict, ProtectHome, PrivateTmp, ProtectKernel*, RestrictNamespaces) that meaningfully reduces blast radius. The lesson closes with what was intentionally left out — reverse proxy and TLS, GPU driver setup, multi-GPU tensor splits, speculative decoding (which empirically does not help Qwen3.6 35B A3B on Ampere), and llama-swap for multi-model rotation — and frames the result as a reproducible private OpenAI-shaped endpoint tunable through one environment file.
